What is CUDA and how does GPU programming differ from CPU programming?

CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA's parallel computing platform extending C/C++ for GPU programming.

**CPU vs GPU design:**
- **CPU**: few powerful cores (4–32), optimized for **latency**, large cache, complex branch prediction
- **GPU**: thousands of simpler cores, optimized for **throughput**, hides latency with massive parallelism

GPU wins on: matrix ops, image processing, neural networks, physics simulations, FFT.
CPU wins on: sequential logic, complex branching, small data, low-latency single tasks.

**GPU hierarchy:**
- **SM** (Streaming Multiprocessor) — fundamental compute unit. Has CUDA cores, warp schedulers, shared memory, L1 cache
- **GPC** (Graphics Processing Cluster) — group of SMs
- **GPU chip** — multiple GPCs + L2 cache + memory controllers + HBM/GDDR6 VRAM

What is a warp in CUDA and why does it matter?

A **warp** is the fundamental execution unit — 32 threads that execute together in lockstep (SIMT — Single Instruction Multiple Thread). All 32 threads execute the same instruction simultaneously.

**Warp scheduler**: each SM has 4 warp schedulers. When one warp stalls (waiting for memory), the scheduler switches to another ready warp — this is how the GPU hides memory latency.

**Occupancy**: ratio of active warps to maximum possible warps per SM. Higher = better latency hiding.

**Warp divergence**: when threads in a warp take different branches (`if/else`), the GPU executes both branches serially with the inactive threads masked out — performance penalty. Minimize divergence within a warp.

What are the NVIDIA GPU compute capability versions?

Compute capability version numbers indicate feature support:
- **6.x**: Pascal (GTX 10xx, P100)
- **7.0**: Volta (V100) — first with tensor cores
- **7.5**: Turing (RTX 20xx)
- **8.0**: Ampere A100; **8.6**: Ampere RTX 30xx
- **8.9**: Ada Lovelace RTX 40xx
- **9.0**: Hopper H100

Examples of real GPUs:
- RTX 3090 (Ampere): 10496 CUDA cores, 82 SMs, 24 GB GDDR6X
- A100: 6912 CUDA cores, 108 SMs, up to 80 GB HBM2e
- H100: 16896 CUDA cores, 132 SMs, 80 GB HBM3

What are the CUDA memory types and which is fastest?

| Memory Type | Location | Speed | Scope | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | SM (on-chip) | Fastest | Thread | ~255/thread |
| Shared memory | SM (on-chip) | ~100× global | Block | 48–164 KB/SM |
| L1/L2 Cache | On-chip / chip | Fast | Auto | varies |
| Constant memory | Device (cached) | Fast if all threads read same addr | All | 64 KB |
| Texture memory | Device (cached) | Fast for 2D spatial locality | All | Large |
| Global memory | HBM/GDDR | Slowest | All | Full VRAM |

```cpp
__shared__ float smem[256];    // shared memory
__constant__ float coeff[64];  // constant memory
__device__ float global_val;   // global device memory
```

**Key insight**: Shared memory is ~100× faster than global memory. The most important CUDA optimization is using shared memory to cache frequently accessed global memory data.
